item.title: China honors international contributors to cultural exchange
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-21 09:02:00
Li Shulei, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and head of the Publicity Department of the CPC Central Committee, attends the 2026 Orchid Awards ceremony and delivers a speech in Beijing, capital of China, Nov. 20, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Ling) China on Friday honored French Nobel laureate in literature Jean-Marie Gustave Le Clézio, renowned Singaporean scholar Kishore Mahbubani, and eight other foreign nationals with its Orchid Awards, recognizing their efforts in facilitating cultural exchanges between China and the rest of the world. The 2026 Orchid Awards ceremony, the third of its kind, was held in Beijing. Li Shulei, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and head of the Publicity Department of the CPC Central Committee, attended the ceremony and delivered a speech. More than 300 people, including representatives of Chinese governmental departments, international organizations, diplomatic envoys in China, and Chinese and foreign think tanks and media organizations, attended Friday's event in the national capital. Participants stressed equality and inclusiveness among different civilizations, calling for efforts to preserve, inherit and pass on human civilizations, and to strengthen digital empowerment to make the progress of civilizations beneficial to all and shared by all. At a regular news briefing, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun congratulated the award recipients, praising their long-term efforts in helping dispel prejudice through culture, deepening understanding via exchange and building people-to-people bridges between China and other countries. The Orchid Awards, established in 2022, aim to recognize international friends and organizations for outstanding contributions to promoting humanity's shared values and mutual learning between Chinese and foreign civilizations. They have become an international cultural platform helping implement the China-proposed Global Civilization Initiative.

item.title: China's high-tech FDI posts strong growth in first 10 months
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-21 08:57:00
A drone photo taken on Nov. 19, 2026 shows a ship arriving at Rizhao Port in east China's Shandong Province. (Xinhua/Guo Xulei) Foreign direct investment (FDI) in China's high-tech industries posted robust year-on-year growth in the first 10 months of 2026, official data showed on Friday. FDI in high-tech industries reached 252.83 billion yuan (about 37.66 billion U.S. dollars) during the January-October period, up 31.3 percent year on year. It accounted for 41.7 percent of China's total FDI in actual use, increasing by 10.7 percentage points from the same period last year, according to the Ministry of Commerce. Specifically, FDI in aerospace and equipment manufacturing, services for the commercialization of sci-tech achievements, and electronic and telecommunications equipment manufacturing surged 128.8 percent, 73.3 percent and 35.7 percent, respectively. A total of 52,853 new foreign-invested enterprises were established nationwide during this period, down 1.7 percent year on year, while FDI in actual use stood at 606.93 billion yuan, declining 2.4 percent from a year earlier. China's manufacturing industry attracted 143.04 billion yuan in FDI in this period, while the service sector drew 450.38 billion yuan. During the same period, FDI from Canada, France, Switzerland and the United States grew by 105.7 percent, 35.1 percent, 23.5 percent and 9.6 percent, respectively, with investment via free ports included in these calculations, the ministry revealed. High-tech and high-value-added industries have increasingly become a key focus for foreign investors in China, a report released in September said. Multinational corporations are accelerating the establishment of R&D centers in China, positioning the country as a vital node in their global innovation networks, the report noted.

item.title: Asia-Pacific Media Partnership officially launched
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-21 08:52:00
CHINA / DIPLOMACY Asia-Pacific Media Partnership officially launched By Xinhua Published: Nov 21, 2026 08:52 AM
The Asia-Pacific Media Partnership (APMP), proposed by China's Xinhua News Agency, has been officially launched, with its first batch of members comprising 310 organizations from 41 countries and regions across the Asia-Pacific. At the opening ceremony of the Asia-Pacific Media Forum held on Sept. 5, more than 400 representatives from over 40 countries and regions, as well as from UN agencies and international organizations, witnessed the establishment of the Organizing Committee of the Asia-Pacific Media Partnership Program. The committee issued an initiative on strengthening collaborative communication between the media and think tanks, inviting media outlets and think tanks in the Asia-Pacific region to join the partnership. Aiming to strengthen mutually beneficial and win-win cooperation among media organizations across the Asia-Pacific region, the APMP focuses on building four key platforms: high-end dialogue, collaborative communication, technological innovation and pragmatic cooperation. It will regularly hold high-level media dialogues, promote joint interviews among Asia-Pacific media, jointly produce high-quality multimedia products, organize inbound reporting tours in China for Asia-Pacific media journalists, and host themed training programs for Asia-Pacific media professionals, among a series of practical cooperation projects. Both the APMP and the Shenzhen Consensus of the Asia-Pacific Media Forum have been officially included in the deliverables list for China's hosting of the 2026 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meetings. The Asia-Pacific Media Forum has also been included in the list of meetings and events hosted by China as the 2026 APEC host.

item.title: Anthropic rings the bell: Why were there no Chinese faces?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-21 00:07:00
File photo VCG On November 19, leading US AI company Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut in what was described as the largest IPO in history, with its market capitalization briefly climbing to nearly $2 trillion. However, among the seven founders who rang the opening bell at the ceremony, not a single Chinese face was present. Many netizens pointed out that while Chinese engineers had made indispensable contributions to Anthropic's growth, gaining access to its board and core decision-making circles remained extremely difficult. This has prompted questions about whether Chinese professionals being shut out of top decision-making positions is an unspoken "rule" in Silicon Valley. Chinese engineers are highly capable technically, but as a whole, they remain concentrated in frontline research and engineering roles, with limited opportunities to advance into the highest levels of corporate decision-making. This is a common problem among US technology companies. Data from US think tanks such as MacroPolo show that, at one point, Chinese researchers (based on undergraduate degrees) accounted for around 38 percent of top-tier AI researchers in the US. In some years, researchers from China even outnumbered those from the US among top-tier AI researchers worldwide. Chinese researchers and engineers are also well represented on the initial team at Meta's Superintelligence Labs and among key research contributors at OpenAI and Anthropic. The technological foundations of these companies rely heavily on Chinese engineers and researchers, while decision-making power remains largely in the hands of founding teams and established networks. There is even a specific term for this phenomenon: the "bamboo ceiling." The stark contrast between Silicon Valley's heavy reliance on Chinese technical talent and the limited representation of Chinese professionals in its top decision-making circles also undermines the Silicon Valley myth that technical excellence alone guarantees equal rewards. Leading technology companies and elite circles have long prided themselves on being "diverse and inclusive." Yet this inclusiveness is, to a considerable extent, reserved for the privileged. From the early days of the semiconductor industry to today's cutting-edge fields of large AI models, computing power and algorithms, numerous Chinese researchers have contributed their expertise. Yet they are often confined to the role of "technical contributors", rarely taking center stage at milestone moments such as IPO bell-ringing events or strategic decision-making forums - platforms that symbolize recognition and a voice in decision-making. This points to a long-standing structural barrier. In recent years, the environment for Chinese technology professionals in Western countries has deteriorated markedly. Prejudice once concealed beneath the rhetoric of "free movement of talent" has increasingly surfaced under the guise of "national security." This policy-level distrust, compounded by heightened scrutiny based on identity amid geopolitical tensions, has further narrowed opportunities for Chinese professionals to advance. In the wake of the controversy surrounding Jensen Huang, some Western media outlets have openly spread the false claim that "all Chinese are spies," fueling anti-China and anti-Chinese rhetoric. In such an atmosphere, Chinese professionals may still be automatically branded as "untrustworthy," no matter how impressive their professional achievements are. At the core of competition for talent is respect for and fair treatment of innovators. An advantage built on suspicion, barriers and exclusionary networks cannot last. Recently, news that Liu Jun, a member of the US National Academy of Sciences, had returned to China to take up a teaching position caused a stir in US public opinion. There is little reason to be surprised. Talent naturally gravitates toward places where the environment is more open, policies are more stable and support systems are more comprehensive. That is simply how the world works.

item.title: 'Thank You, China' from world leaders is more than just a courtesy: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-21 00:00:00
This photo taken on November 16, 2026 shows a view of Shenzhen, South China's Guangdong Province with APEC elements. China will hold the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen from November 18 to 19. Photo: VCG Behind the widely shared expressions of "Thank you, China" lies not only an expectation of further cooperation, but also a vote of confidence in China as a reliable partner. As the host, China patiently built bridges of communication, responding to major economies' concerns over industrial chain stability and technological innovation while listening to the pressing needs of developing members for infrastructure, capacity building and green transition. The 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting has successfully concluded. Before heading home, leaders from various economies expressed their sincere gratitude to Chinese President Xi Jinping, China, the host of this meeting, and the city of Shenzhen. Russian President Vladimir Putin said he "congratulates" Chinese friends' hosting of a "very successful APEC summit." US President Donald Trump said that if the highest possible score were 10, he would give his visit to China "a 12." Leaders from Vietnam, South Korea, Malaysia, Thailand and Canada, as well as representatives of international organizations and other participants, also spoke highly of the achievements of China's APEC Year and expressed their appreciation for the excellent work of the Chinese side. It is hard to say goodbye after a visit to Shenzhen. The Shenzhen APEC meeting has left a distinctive mark on the history of APEC and a lasting impression on the hearts and minds of participating economies across the Asia-Pacific. During the Shenzhen meeting, leaders of various economies created many heartwarming moments as they stepped out of conference venues and into the city's streets. Beyond the meeting rooms, the streets of Shenzhen became places for unexpected encounters. Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, whose ancestral roots trace back to Guangdong Province, showed off his Cantonese skills on several occasions. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese sampled beef at a supermarket, while Mexico's Secretary of Health David Kershenobich Stalnikowitz visited Huaqiangbei, a bustling commercial district popular with international visitors. These heartwarming moments not only became trending topics on Chinese social media, but also left fond memories for guests from various sides who had traveled from afar. Behind the widely shared expressions of "Thank you, China" lies not only an expectation of further cooperation, but also a vote of confidence in China as a reliable partner. At a time when protectionism is on the rise and global economic growth is under pressure, bringing 21 APEC member economies together around the same table is no easy task. This is all the more challenging given the vast differences in their economic size, stages of development and diverse interests. An equal platform for dialogue and in-depth discussion is therefore all the more necessary. As the host, China patiently built bridges of communication, responding to major economies' concerns over industrial chain stability and technological innovation while listening to the pressing needs of developing members in infrastructure, capacity building and green transition. Leaders from various economies consistently praised China's thoughtful and efficient organization, as well as the candid and pragmatic atmosphere for communication. The meeting also forged tangible consensus. From the Suzhou Statement at the APEC Ministers Responsible for Trade Meeting to the Chengdu Statement at the APEC Digital and AI Ministerial Meeting, from the Nanjing Statement at the APEC Human Resources Development Ministerial Meeting to 2026 APEC Leaders' Shenzhen Outlook at the Economic Leaders' Meeting, China placed economic and trade cooperation, innovation and people's livelihoods at the heart of its year-long APEC agenda. A total of 321 meetings and events and 75 major deliverables have provided more concrete avenues for Asia-Pacific cooperation, injecting fresh vitality and strong momentum into regional development. Some foreign media outlets have noted that, against a backdrop of mounting global geopolitical tensions, the Shenzhen meeting was one of the "few forums" capable of bringing "together" economies of different sizes. These achievements reflect the host's year-long commitment and demonstrate that, by identifying common interests, economies can continue to unleash the vitality and potential of the Asia-Pacific economy and advance the building of an Asia-Pacific community. Many leaders and foreign media outlets have praised Shenzhen, remarking that every time they come, it looks different. Shenzhen itself also offers the world a glimpse of how China is advancing high-standard opening-up. Having grown amid China's reform and opening-up, Shenzhen has now become a key node in global industrial chains and innovation networks. By hosting the APEC meeting in Shenzhen and announcing new funding for APEC practical cooperation to launch new cooperation institutions covering digital technology, cross-border data flow, clean energy, and the development of SMEs, China shows its sincerity in committing resources and sharing development opportunities. Asia-Pacific economies vary widely in their stages of development. Some prioritize market access, while others are in urgent need of infrastructure and talent. China brings these diverse needs into a single cooperation agenda, enabling all parties to find pathways for participation. This vision carries substantial practical weight. The trust that Asia-Pacific partners place in China also stems from China's strategic resolve to take root in the Asia-Pacific, contribute to its development and deliver benefits to the region. China outlined the way forward in Shenzhen, facilitated agreement among all parties on concrete actions, and readied resources and platforms to implement those actions. These efforts have shown all parties that China is willing to listen to the concerns of different economies, has the ability to coordinate their respective interests, and demonstrates a sense of responsibility in advancing shared goals. Against narratives that frame economic ties as burdens and interdependence as risks, China continues to expand openness for the long-term interests of the entire Asia-Pacific. The dynamism of the Asia-Pacific economy stems from decades of close exchanges between people and enterprises. To preserve these connections is to safeguard shared opportunities for growth. Further recognition of the Shenzhen APEC meeting will translate into easier trade, smoother exchanges and broader access to innovative opportunities ahead. The gratitude expressed to China by participants in Shenzhen grows out of trust built through cooperation. China's actions over the year demonstrate that the more complex the international landscape becomes, the more the Asia-Pacific can find a sincere, reliable and capable leader on the path of open cooperation.

item.title: Chinese AI tools support emissions monitoring and climate resilience while building local expertise across Global South
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-20 21:53:00
A humanoid robot made by Unitree Robotics performs outside the China Pavilion at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, in November 2026. Photo: IC In a vineyard in Lebanon's Bekaa Valley, Chinese and Lebanese researchers attached sensors to grapevines to measure water moving through their stems. The fieldwork, carried out in June 2023 by a Chinese team led by Zhu Weiwei of the Aerospace Information Research Institute (AIR), Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), formed part of a wider effort to understand agricultural water consumption. Lebanese technicians also received training in maintaining instruments, receiving observations and processing the resulting data. Following water through a single vine might seem a long way from international climate negotiations. Yet such measurements help answer a practical question facing water-scarce regions: how much water do crops actually consume, and how can that information guide its use? The ground observations provide a reference for interpreting satellite measurements. Combined with artificial intelligence and physical models, they allow researchers to extend their analysis beyond individual plants and fields to irrigation districts and entire river basins. As the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) enters its final scheduled day in Antalya, Türkiye, negotiators are working to bridge differences over climate finance, adaptation and emissions reductions. A new draft of the conference's overarching decision, released on November 19, has provided a basis for the final-stage consultations. China has also brought AI applications to COP31, showcasing tools for emissions monitoring, disaster early warning and clean energy management. Against this backdrop, Chinese scientists are connecting environmental observations with practical tools to support emissions cuts and strengthen climate resilience, particularly in developing countries. Following water from a vine to a river basin For the researchers working in Lebanon, the vineyard was one part of a larger observation network. Instruments were installed across different landscapes in the Bekaa Valley, including farmland, orchards and mixed woodland, to examine exchanges of water and heat between the land and atmosphere. Measurements from such sites help researchers check whether satellite-based estimates capture actual conditions. They also reveal differences that might be obscured when a large area is treated as a uniform landscape. AIR's ETWatch system and its cloud platform combine ground observations with satellite information, AI and physical models to estimate evapotranspiration — water returning to the atmosphere through evaporation from surfaces and transpiration by plants. Knowing this consumption is important when assessing water conservation. Researchers need to establish whether an intervention reduces total water consumed across a basin, and how irrigation changes that consumption relative to natural conditions. A cloud platform makes the analysis accessible beyond the research team that developed it. According to AIR's material, related methods have been applied in more than 40 river basins. The team has also organized technical training for participants from countries including Egypt, Mozambique, Uzbekistan and Brazil. Experience in another AIR program shows why the field component matters. On an early visit to farmland in Mozambique, remote sensing researcher Zhang Miao encountered plots so overgrown that he initially struggled to recognize them as cultivated fields. Grass could be as abundant as the crops themselves, he recalled. For crop monitoring, that creates a consequential ambiguity. A satellite may detect dense green vegetation, but some of the signal may come from weeds. Interpreting it as healthy crop growth could produce an overly optimistic harvest estimate. The experience helps explain why sharing an algorithm is only part of international scientific cooperation. Reliable monitoring also requires knowledge of local crops, farming practices and landscapes, supported by observations that allow models to be checked and adjusted. Forecasting adds another dimension to water management: time to prepare. The Chinese researchers are working with the Water Resources Research Institute of Egypt's National Water Research Center to combine AI methods with dynamical climate models for Nile flow predictions two to six weeks ahead. Demonstration applications are planned for the 2027 flood season, the Global Times learned from the CAS' Institute of Atmospheric Physics (IAP). That timescale falls between conventional weather forecasts and seasonal outlooks. Information about likely changes in river flow can support preparations for irrigation, water supply and reservoir operations, where decisions must often be made before the next rainfall arrives. For coastal countries exposed to tropical cyclones, researchers are also examining how AI can better represent uncertainty. An IAP team and collaborators combined the FuXi weather model with a physics-based approach to generate alternative cyclone forecasts. Tests showed improvements in track prediction and uncertainty assessment, helping explore a storm's possible developments rather than relying on a single projected path. Across these applications, observations and forecasts serve different stages of preparation. Agricultural water monitoring examines what has been consumed; river and weather predictions help anticipate what may come next. Building forecasts together When Thai meteorological experts arrived in Xiong'an in August, they brought a shared research task to their Chinese counterparts: examining how an AI forecasting system performed when predicting temperatures and rainfall in Thailand, including during extreme weather. Working alongside researchers at the Xiong'an Meteorological AI Innovation Institute in North China's Hebei Province, the visiting specialists began evaluating forecasts of daily average temperatures, maximum temperatures and precipitation. The work moved their newly established joint laboratory from a cooperation agreement into day-to-day research, according to materials provided by the institute to the Global Times. The China-Thailand Joint Laboratory for Intelligent Prediction and Early Warning of Meteorological Disasters was launched on July 17 at a meteorological forum during the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai. Jointly led by the Xiong'an institute and the Thai Meteorological Department's Climate Center, it has Chinese and Thai co-directors and brings together more than 40 experts in fields including atmospheric science, AI, agriculture and electricity systems. The researchers are targeting a particularly useful but challenging forecasting window: several weeks to months ahead. Earlier information about heavy rainfall, drought and extreme heat could give farmers, power operators and infrastructure managers more time to prepare. Making those forecasts useful requires adapting global models to local conditions. The teams have been testing the Fengshun AI prediction system over Thailand, examining its performance during extreme events and using nearly 20 years of retrospective forecasts to develop corrections. Their work also aims to refine forecasts to a grid spacing of 10 kilometers, providing more detailed information for regional warnings. The cooperation builds on years of exchanges between the two countries' meteorological services. According to the institute's materials, the Chinese side has provided more than 320 training participations for Thai meteorological personnel, including 67 in-person training visits to China, and hosted two Thai visiting scholars. The joint laboratory gives that exchange a continuing research framework. Thai specialists work with Chinese colleagues to evaluate the model's performance and develop forecasts suited to their country's needs, while the Chinese side shares prediction systems, data and research infrastructure. Fengshun has already supplied experimental forecast products to Thailand. The next stage is to bring the jointly developed methods closer to routine forecasting: the partners plan to deploy an upgraded version in Thailand in 2027 and integrate their research into the MAZU early warning system for operational trials. A meteorological AI workshop scheduled for November 23-25 in Xiong'an will include a dedicated session on the laboratory. For the two teams, the work ahead includes checking how their models handle Thailand's rainfall and heat extremes, correcting errors and testing whether the resulting forecasts can support local warning services. Experience with CropWatch shows how sustained training can change who produces the information used in national decisions. After the cloud platform became available to Mozambique in 2017, local technicians spent the following three years learning to operate it independently, analyze crop conditions and incorporate their findings into national agro-meteorological bulletins in Portuguese. AI is now helping CropWatch users generate draft analytical reports. Those drafts still require professional review, team member Zhang Miao told the Global Times, making local expertise essential to interpreting results before they reach decision-makers. The next round of small island training is planned for December 7-11 in Sanya, South China's Hainan Province. Jointly organized by the International Research Center of Big Data for Sustainable Development Goals (CBAS) and the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs, it will focus on using AI-driven Big Earth Data to strengthen national capacity to implement sustainable development priorities. Participants will work on bringing the technology into the institutions responsible for decisions at home. From data to action At the China Pavilion at COP31, a wheeled robot dog patrols an exhibition area, collecting images, sounds and gas data. The demonstration shows how mobile equipment could support emissions inspections. Nearby, visitors can interact with virtual volunteers answering carbon-market policy questions in multiple languages. A connected AI system demonstrates how it can assist with checking carbon-market data and flagging potential problems. Organized by the Ministry of Ecology and Environment's information center, the exhibition brings together monitoring equipment and digital systems used to support climate governance. Wang Haiyang, director of the center, explained that China is developing carbon-market AI models and agents that combine multiple data sources with regulatory rules to assist emissions accounting, data checks and compliance assessments. On November 11, China unveiled an integrated hardware and software package for its MAZU meteorological early warning solution in a video presentation at COP31's high-level forum on South-South cooperation on climate change, CCTV News reported. The compact hardware and software package allows developing countries to connect local observations with forecasting and warning services. It can operate independently or connect with cloud resources and existing systems. A version delivered to Sri Lanka on November 1 includes customized aviation and marine modules and is expected to enter operational use by the end of 2026, according to the China Meteorological Administration. By October 2026, the broader MAZU solution had been deployed in eight countries, including Pakistan, Ethiopia and Sri Lanka, with cloud-based trials underway in more than 50 countries, according to the China Meteorological Administration. Other Chinese presentations addressed a challenge created by AI itself: how to supply reliable clean electricity to increasingly power-hungry computing facilities. At a November 14 China Pavilion side event, Chinese solar and storage company LONGi discussed how to match renewable electricity with computing demand. Solar and wind output fluctuate, while data centers require continuous power, making the timing of electricity supply a central concern. At a November 13 COP31 side event focused on adaptation in African least developed countries, the company also presented an integrated solar and storage solution managed through AI software. Its representatives discussed projects in countries including Nigeria, Mozambique and Zimbabwe, alongside local training and maintenance support. The practical needs they described included keeping vaccines refrigerated and water pumps running. Whatever the final outcome of the negotiations in Antalya, these applications offer a silver lining.

item.title: GT on the spot: From AI remixes to tea livestreams, young people bring fresh energy to ethnic unity in Yunnan
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-20 21:04:00
Visitors experience the relaxed pace of life in Nuogan village on Jingmai Mountain in Pu'er, Southwest China's Yunnan Province. Photo: Li Hao/Global Times A Jingpo melody from Southwest China's Yunnan Province has found a new life on phone screens. Reworked with artificial intelligence and paired with striking dance videos, it has encouraged people far beyond its birthplace to follow the rhythm and discover the culture behind it. On Jingmai Mountain in Pu'er, another screen connects viewers with a different tradition. Xianjin, an ethnic Dai woman born in the 2000s, uses livestreams to talk about her hometown's tea, ancient forests and village life. During a recent reporting tour in Yunnan, Global Times reporter explored how younger generations are creating opportunities for exchange among ethnic groups, bringing fresh energy to efforts to forge a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation. Lyrics of the soil At Longchuan's Munao Zongge square in Dehong Dai and Jingpo Autonomous Prefecture, Yunnan, local dancers in ethnic dress and visitors form long lines, moving to the same beat. The procession brings people together in an activity they can join without being professional performers or belonging to a particular ethnic group. The viral music has deep roots, but its present form is a recent creation. Jingpo artist Shi Legan composed the "Munao Zongge March" in 1991. Earlier this year, Beijing musician Zhen Zhen adapted that melody with new lyrics and AI-assisted arrangements and vocals. Without A-list celebrities or professional promotional campaigns, the song "Munao Zongge" has garnered nearly 3 billion views on China's major short-video platform Douyin. Munao Zongge, a major Jingpo celebration featuring collective dancing, was included in China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2006. Its winding dance formations carry memories of the Jingpo people's migration, giving today's online enthusiasm a connection to a much longer history. The name carries the idea of gathering to sing and dance. During major celebrations, participants from neighboring ethnic groups also share a meal served on banana leaves, extending the gathering from the dance ground to the dining table. For Zhen, a video of mass dancing prompted an interest that became three weeks of work. Research changed his understanding of the music: early attempts to treat it as a love song gave way to lyrics informed by Jingpo history. AI helped him arrange the music and produce virtual voices, but its research results sometimes conflicted. He went back to books and papers to check the information himself. "Lyrics have to grow out of the soil," Zhen said. In Longchuan, community dance leader Song Haihe introduced that participants include locals from different ethnic groups alongside visitors from across the country. The cultural interest also brings visitors to local businesses. Longchuan received 42,000 domestic tourist visits during this year's National Day holiday, while overnight stays in commercial accommodation rose 11.07 percent year-on-year, according to the county's culture and tourism authorities. For someone first drawn to the music through a short video, these regular gatherings provide a place to learn its steps alongside local people. The encounter can continue after the video ends. Xianjin welcomes visitors to her family's tea shop in Nuogan village. Photo: Li Hao/Global Times Connections over tea On Jingmai Mountain, Xianjin faces a related task: giving people who discover her hometown online a reason to understand it more closely. An encounter at a tea exhibition in 2020 exposed a problem she would have to overcome. When she introduced tea from her hometown, a trader asked: "Where is Jingmai Mountain?" Having a distinctive product did not guarantee that buyers knew its origins. After returning home, she began livestreaming to introduce the tea and its place of origin. Her days combine brewing tea, making tea-flavored ice cream and filming village life. She opened a tea house after seeing more visitors arrive following the mountain's World Heritage inscription in 2023. Early in her business, she realized that selling the name "Jingmai tea" was insufficient. Her videos began showing what distinguished its place of origin: clouds over the mountain, hand-processing techniques and daily life in traditional houses. The landscape behind those sales is itself a product of longstanding cooperation. UNESCO describes Jingmai Mountain's tea-growing system as having developed over more than a thousand years through the practices of the Blang and Dai peoples. Tea grows beneath a forest canopy, within a landscape of villages, groves and protective forests. Local authorities told the Global Times that the inscribed heritage area includes five old tea forests, nine traditional villages and three protective partition forests. Protecting the trees also means maintaining the communities and knowledge that have sustained them. During the reporting tour, Xianjin pointed to renovated old houses and explained that residents of different ethnic groups had worked to preserve them. The forests and village buildings were a shared inheritance. Jingmai village official Yan Sailuan described cooperation that extends from celebrations to farm work. People gather in one another's villages for festivals, contribute labor and organize long-table banquets; during tea picking and other agricultural work, neighbors help one another. Skills circulate through the same relationships. In Wengji village, tea-processing heritage practitioner Sanwen teaches learners from different villages and ethnic groups. His workshop has also become a place where visitors can experience traditional tea making. The opportunities extend beyond individual businesses. Jingmai Mountain received 694,300 tourist visits in 2025, with culture and tourism revenue reaching 563 million yuan ($84.45 million). Residents have converted traditional homes into tea shops, restaurants and guesthouses, retaining the buildings' distinctive appearance while finding new uses for them. The younger generation is adding new partners to these networks. Xia Haoling, who previously worked in branding and new media in Shanghai, settled on Jingmai Mountain and established the Zhishan brand, developing scented sachets and incense inspired by local plants and Blang culture. The growing business has changed everyday logistics, too. Previously, tea sold online had to be packed late into the night and taken down to the township for dispatch the next morning. Couriers now come up to the village regularly to collect parcels. For Xianjin, the ancient forests remain the starting point of these new ventures. "These roots belong to all of us, whichever ethnic group we come from," she said.

item.title: Chinese boys, aged 14 and 3, set BMX and cartwheel records for Guinness World Records Day
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-20 17:28:00
Liu Haoran November 19 marked the 22nd annual Guinness World Records Day. Challengers from around the world pushed the limits of human capability once again on the same day. Among them, two challengers from China attracted considerable attention: a 14-year-old who performed 10 consecutive flips in the air while riding a BMX bike, and a 3-year-old who performed 55 cartwheels in one minute on the ground. In China, 14-year-old BMX freestyle rider Liu Haoran set two records during this year's Guinness World Records Day challenge: "Most consecutive BMX side somersaults" (10 consecutive flips) and "Highest BMX backflip" (3.13 meters). Liu also improved on his own previous world record. A BMX backflip is a freestyle trick in which the rider and bike rotate 360 degrees backward mid-air off a ramp or jump before landing on the wheels. The flair is a highly difficult maneuver in BMX freestyle. Riders must launch themselves into the air on a ramp, simultaneously flipping themselves and their bikes sideways before landing precisely back down the ramp. Peng Yizhou The other challenger from China, Peng Yizhou, 3, a martial arts school student, completed 55 sidecar flips in one minute during this year's challenge, setting a Guinness World Record for the most cartwheels in one minute in the under 16 category. Peng was born in Tangyin County, Anyang City, Central China's Henan Province. His parents are both martial arts instructors. From the age of 7 months, Peng lived with his parents at a martial arts school, watching the older students practice martial arts. At the age of 2, he began to imitate cartwheels on his own and gradually learned to perform the movement independently under his father's guidance. In addition to cartwheels, he also enjoys swimming, playing with toys, and participating in activities with the older students at the martial arts school. For Peng, the cartwheel wasn't initially a competitive skill he needed to master; rather, it stemmed from curiosity and imitation of his surroundings. His parents recalled that when Peng first completed a cartwheel independently, he tried repeatedly, falling several times, until finally landing steadily and excitedly turning to his father, shouting, "Dad, I stood up!" Global Times

item.title: Time for Takaichi to retract her erroneous 'survival-threatening situation' remarks
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-20 12:35:00
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi speaks to reporters ahead of her departure for a tour of Europe at the Prime Minister's Official Residence in Tokyo on June 13, 2026. Photo: VCG On November 19, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi held a press conference after attending the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, reiterating that Japan's basic position on the Taiwan question remains consistent with the 1972 Sino-Japanese Joint Statement and emphasizing that "there has been absolutely no change to this position." She also said that "China is an important neighboring country," that the status of the four political documents as the "basic documents on Japan-China relations" remains unchanged, and that Japan is willing to comprehensively advance a strategic relationship of mutual benefit through dialogue and build "constructive and stable" China-Japan relations. However, when asked about with her erroneous remarks a year earlier that the Chinese mainland's "use of force on Taiwan" could constitute a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan, Takaichi continued to evade the question, saying that "she could not comment on hypothetical scenarios." The core principles of the Sino-Japanese Joint Statement are clearly set out in black and white: The Government of Japan recognizes that the Government of the People's Republic of China as the sole legal Government of China. The Government of the People's Republic of China reiterates that Taiwan is an inalienable part of the territory of the People's Republic of China. The Government of Japan fully understands and respects this stand of the Government of the People's Republic of China, and it firmly maintains its stand under Article 8 of the Postdam Proclamation. This statement, together with the other four political documents, including the Treaty of Peace and Friendship between China and Japan, forms the political foundation for the normalization of diplomatic relations between the two countries. These are commitments that both countries must uphold in their bilateral relations and an important part of the postwar international order. Linking a "contingency in Taiwan" to a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan and implying that Japan might exercise its right to collective self-defense directly undermines the framework established by the 1972 Sino-Japanese Joint Statement and seriously deviates from the postwar international order that Japan, as a defeated nation in World War II, is obliged to observe. If Japan's position on the Taiwan question is truly consistent with the Sino-Japan Joint Statement, it should acknowledge its mistake and publicly retract the provocative claim that "a Taiwan contingency is a Japan contingency." On the same day, the leaders of China, Russia and the US held a historic trilateral meeting in Shenzhen and issued the China-Russia-US Heads of State Declaration toward Peace. All three leaders recalled the history of their countries fighting side by side during World War II, sending an important signal of their shared commitment to safeguarding the postwar international order - a message that Tokyo should take note of. The core documents underpinning the postwar international order include the Cairo Declaration and the Potsdam Proclamation, which made clear that Japan must return the Chinese territories it had seized, including Taiwan. Japan accepted the Potsdam Proclamation and surrendered unconditionally, and subsequently reaffirmed its commitment to adhering to Article 8 of the proclamation in the Sino-Japan Joint Statement. Any remarks that directly link the Taiwan question to Japan's security, or even imply possible military intervention, constitute an open challenge to the outcomes of the victory in World War II and the postwar international order. China-Japan relations remain strained over remarks concerning Taiwan, with tensions already affecting economic and trade ties, people-to-people exchanges and other areas. Takaichi has emphasized dialogue and a strategic relationship of mutual benefit, but her words must be matched by actions. If she sincerely wishes to improve China-Japan relations, retracting her erroneous remarks should be the first step. Otherwise, merely repeating that Japan's "position remains unchanged" without making substantive corrections will do little to inspire confidence or benefit Japan itself, or contribute to lasting peace and stability in the region.

item.title: 30 DR Congo female students awarded China's Mulan Scholarship
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-20 11:59:00
Chinese Ambassador to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) Zhao Bin presents certificates and scholarships to representative recipients in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Nov. 18, 2026. A total of 30 female students from the DRC were awarded the Mulan Scholarship at a ceremony held Wednesday in Kinshasa by the Chinese Embassy, marking the fifth edition of an initiative aimed at supporting women's education and empowerment in the Central African country.
